bib.title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

question: What are the open problems and fundamental limitations of RLHF and related methods, how can they be understood, mitigated and complemented, and what disclosure standards would support oversight?
contributions: Concrete challenges with RLHF: taxonomy of problems with human feedback, reward model and policy, split into tractable vs fundamental (Sec 3)
Incorporating RLHF into a broader technical safety framework (Sec 4)
Governance and transparency: disclosure details that would support auditing (Sec 5)

results.claim: Comparison-based feedback yields policies with high median rather than high mean performance: with A always worth 1 and B worth 10 on 40% of examples but judged 0 on 60%, preferences favour A though B has higher expected reward (4 vs 1).
results.setup: Toy example of binary preference feedback.
results.quote: 40% of examples but are overlooked and concluded to have value 0 on 60%.

results.claim: Paper taxonomises 3 stages (feedback, reward model, policy) plus joint training; each challenge is labelled tractable (fixable within RLHF) or fundamental (needs non-RLHF approach or compensating safety measures); the split is soft.
results.setup: Qualitative taxonomy, Sec 3 and Appendix B.
results.quote: This distinction is soft, and some categories of challenges are marginal.

results.claim: Without a KL penalty to the base model, LLMs under RL often output nonsensical text; proxy over-optimisation hurts the true goal.
results.source: Ziegler et al. 2019; Stiennon et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2022
results.setup: RL fine-tuning of LMs against learned reward.
results.quote: LLMs undergoing RL often learn to output nonsensical text

results.claim: Recommended strategy is defense in depth: several safety measures with uncorrelated failure modes rather than relying on RLHF alone.
results.quote: A better approach is defense in depth: multiple safety measures with uncorrelated failure modes.

limits: Survey with no new experiments; the numbers are quoted from cited work.
Tractable vs fundamental categorisation is explicitly soft, with some marginal cases.
Focus is mostly LLMs but many examples come from robotics/control RL.
Written mid-2023: DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) is mentioned only as supervised alternative; later RLAIF, verifiable-reward RL not covered.
Authors concede many problems are not unique to RLHF so uncorrelated safety measures may be hard to find.
Does not specify implementation hyperparameters; Eq. 1-3 are a simplified framework the authors say misses reality (App A).
practices: Treat RLHF as one layer in defense in depth, not a complete alignment solution (Sec 4).
Regularise the policy with a KL penalty to the base model to avoid nonsensical reward-hacked output (Sec 3.2.2).
Refresh preference labels periodically during policy training and tune that interval; monitor KL shift or reward-ensemble disagreement to detect over-optimisation (Sec 3.4).
Use diverse, adversarial and reward-model-uncertain examples for feedback data (Sec 3.1.3).
Consider multi-objective or multimodal reward models and modelling multiple evaluators rather than treating disagreement as noise (Sec 4.2.2, 3.2.1).
Use ensembles of reward models to maintain uncertainty (Sec 4.2.2).
Consider fine-grained feedback and process supervision for multi-step tasks (Sec 4.2.1).
Red-team and adversarially train against jailbreaks; RLHF is not designed for adversarial robustness (Sec 4.3).
Disclose pretraining data, evaluator selection and training, example selection, feedback type, QA measures, reward and policy loss, evaluation results, audits and expected risks (Sec 5, Fig 4).

terms.definition: methods that combine three interconnected processes: feedback collection, reward modeling, and policy optimization
relatively tractable and could reasonably be addressed within the RLHF framework using improved methodology
substantial enough that overcoming them would require a method that is no longer a form of RLHF
the ability to effectively supervise models given limited resources and bandwidth
RL-trained language models pandering to evaluators' biases
RL finetuning decreases the diversity of samples produced by a model
applying strong optimization pressure for an imperfect proxy measure for a goal tends to cause poor performance on the underlying target goal
when reward and policy are learned jointly from policy samples, features with overestimated rewards become more present in feedback data and underestimated ones disappear
